subject: surgery
title: Intermittent Claudication and Peripheral Arterial Disease

steps.tx: Cramping leg pain brought on by walking and relieved by rest is **intermittent claudication**. Narrowed arteries cannot increase blood flow to exercising muscle, so pain builds at a predictable distance. Stopping lets supply meet demand again and pain fades within minutes. Students should connect this fact with the presenting symptoms, since examination questions usually test that clinical link directly.
steps.say: Intermittent claudication causes cramping calf pain at a predictable walking distance, relieved by rest.

vis.alt: Peripheral arterial disease narrowing leg arteries.
vis.caption: Peripheral arterial disease of the legs. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Pain in the foot at rest, worse lying flat, signals advanced disease called **rest pain**. It means blood flow cannot meet even resting tissue needs. Patients often hang the leg out of bed at night to ease it with gravity. Documenting this finding clearly in the notes guides the next clinician and supports safe, well planned further management.
steps.say: Rest pain means flow cannot meet resting needs, and patients hang the leg down at night for relief.

steps.tx: The ratio of ankle to arm systolic pressure is the **ankle brachial pressure index**. Values below 0.9 indicate arterial narrowing, and very low values mean severe disease. It is measured with a Doppler probe and blood pressure cuff. When this picture is seen in practice, urgent senior review is wise whenever there is any doubt about severity.
steps.say: The ankle brachial pressure index compares ankle and arm pressures, with low values meaning severe disease.

steps.tx: Absent foot pulses with pale, cool skin and shiny hairless legs are typical **examination findings**. Comparing both legs side by side reveals temperature and colour differences. Capillary return is slow in the affected foot. Understanding this mechanism explains the symptoms, the investigation findings and the logic behind each step of treatment given.
steps.say: Absent pulses, cool pale skin and slow capillary return mark the affected leg on examination.

vis.caption: Arterial disease of the extremities. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Stopping smoking is the single most effective step in **risk factor control**. Diabetes, blood pressure and cholesterol treatment slow progression throughout the body. Antiplatelet and statin therapy reduce heart attacks and strokes in these patients. This distinction changes management, so it should be settled early rather than after empirical treatment has already begun.
steps.say: Stopping smoking plus antiplatelet and statin therapy slows progression and prevents heart events.

steps.tx: Structured walking that pushes into pain and rests repeatedly is **supervised exercise therapy**. Over weeks it lengthens pain free walking distance as collateral vessels develop. It rivals stenting for many patients with claudication alone. Careful history taking and examination help place this finding in the right clinical context before treatment is planned.
steps.say: Supervised walking therapy lengthens pain free distance as collateral vessels develop over weeks.

steps.tx: Imaging the arterial tree before intervention is done by **CT angiography**. It maps narrowings and blockages from aorta to foot. The map lets surgeons choose between balloon treatment and bypass. Correlating this finding with imaging and laboratory results prevents both delayed treatment and unnecessary intervention in most patients.
steps.say: CT angiography maps narrowings from aorta to foot so surgeons can choose balloon or bypass.

steps.tx: Ulcers and black toes in a claudicant mean disease has reached **tissue loss**. This stage needs urgent vascular assessment and usually revascularisation. Delay risks spreading infection and major amputation. Early recognition matters because timely treatment gives clearly better outcomes than waiting for complications to develop first.
steps.say: Ulcers and black toes mean tissue loss needing urgent vascular assessment and revascularisation.

steps.tx: Sudden painful pale pulseless leg is acute limb ischaemia, distinct from chronic **claudication history**. It is an emergency with only hours to save the leg. Any sudden change in a claudicant needs same day vascular review. Students should connect this fact with the presenting symptoms, since examination questions usually test that clinical link directly.
steps.say: A suddenly painful pale pulseless leg is an emergency distinct from chronic claudication.
